newsitem.title: MOROCCO: Morocco looks to lead emerging markets league.
newsitem.headline: Morocco looks to lead emerging markets league.

text.p: Morocco's economic leaders outlined a framework of reforms and billion dollar projects on Thursday aimed at putting the North African country at the top of emerging markets for future investment.

Andre Azoulay, economic adviser to Moroccan King Hassan, told nearly 400 delegates from 18 countries: "For us, the fast development of our capital markets is, before every other aim, crucial to helping Moroccan companies compete in the new free trade zone Morocco is building."
Morocco has an accord with the European Union to dismantle all non-agricultural trade with Europe by the year 2009.

Speaking of change to provide finance through the markets, Azoulay said: "Market capitalisation has almost quadrupled from 1992 to 1996 -- from $2.4 billion to $9 billion. Yearly volume has multiplied...from $110 million to $2.2 billion..."
Reforms had led to barring commercial banks from brokerage, privatisation of the stock exchange, a securities exchange commission, and the framework for the mutual funds industry.
"We are currently launching a central custodian to improve settlement procedures...the private Casablanca stock exchange is moving to a computerized trading system.

"We are putting all our efforts in the development of an efficient domestic debt market, both for treasury and corporate issuers; the secondary market and legal framework for securitisation is under study," he added.
Morocco planned to redesign the pension system to improve long-term savings, he said, a point taken up by Finance Minister Mohamed Kabbaj.

Kabbaj told delegates at the Euromoney capital markets and investment forum that greater saving was essential and the aim was to raise it to 25 percent of gross domestic product (GDP) from the current 18 to 20 percent.
"This current level is relatively weak and is an obstacle to the realisation of sustained growth," he said, adding that he was looking especially at life assurance and pension funds.

Another speaker, Stuart Brown, from Banque Paribas, pointed out that fast growing economies saved between 30 and 40 percent of GDP. Morocco needed further reform such as full liberalisation of deposit rates and expansion of the secondary market for Treasury bills.

Kabbaj said Morocco's growth strategy focused on efforts to consolidate macro-economic balance, strengthen the private sector role, consolidate business law, and pursue development strategies to cut social and regional differences.
About half its 27 million people live in the countryside where many have no access to electricity, piped water, and where levels of literacy are low.

The minister said Morocco was engaged in a programme of concessions to the private sector to provide and manage public services and facilities like distribution of electricity and water, energy, highways, ports and telecommunications.
